claims.text: Local lattice distortions caused by atomic-size mismatch are the primary factor governing superconducting properties in non-Nb–Ta-dominant high-entropy alloys.
The proposed starting material is a single-phase, disordered, titanium-rich heavy-transition-metal solid solution containing at least five elements at 5 at.% or more each and is not Nb–Ta dominant.
Substitution by an element with similar electronic character but a different atomic radius can vary local lattice distortion.
Using substituents of similar electronic character will keep the electron count nearly constant.
Identical processing conditions can ensure that all comparison samples remain single-phase solid solutions.
Variations in lattice parameters can provide evidence of local lattice distortion.
Short-range chemical order can provide evidence of the degree of local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortion modulates the microscopic electronic environment.
Atomic-size mismatch induces local lattice strain.
Local lattice strain alters electron–phonon coupling strength.
Local lattice strain alters the density of states at the Fermi level.
Moderate lattice distortion can enhance superconducting pairing interactions.
A moderate increase in atomic-size mismatch will raise the superconducting transition temperature relative to the starting alloy.
A moderate increase in atomic-size mismatch will raise the upper critical field relative to the starting alloy.
Excessive lattice distortion may disrupt superconducting coherence and suppress superconductivity.
The starting titanium-rich alloy has minimal atomic-size mismatch and well-characterized Tc and Hc2 values.
The proposed relationship is restricted to bulk, single-phase solid solutions without intermetallic precipitation or phase separation.
Absence of a systematic correlation between measured lattice distortion and Tc or Hc2 would falsify the claim that lattice distortion governs superconductivity in the proposed alloy series.
